chief_complaint: excruciating, out-of-proportion leg pain, severe pain on passive stretch of toes, and tense woody calf swelling 12 hours after tibial fracture
hpi_details: 29M with casted tibial fracture complaining of agonizing 10/10 leg pain unresponsive to opioids with exquisite pain on passive ankle dorsiflexion where compartment pressure measures 45 mmHg requiring immediate emergent bivalving of cast and four-compartment fasciotomy.
ideas: He thinks the plaster cast was wrapped far too tightly around his lower leg and is cutting off all blood flow to his foot.
concerns: He is terrified that the cut-off circulation will cause permanent nerve damage or force doctors to amputate his leg.
expectations: He hopes the doctors will cut the cast off immediately and give him a much stronger painkiller that actually gives him relief.

investigation_events.availability_message: The compartment pressure measurement is now available. A clear clinical diagnosis should not be delayed for repeated measurements.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Acute Compartment Syndrome evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute Compartment Syndrome is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes Evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocol for Acute Compartment Syndrome Lower Extremity Fracture, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: excruciating, out-of-proportion leg pain, severe pain on passive stretch of toes, and tense woody calf swelling 12 hours after tibial fracture

Key HPI features: 29M with casted tibial fracture complaining of agonizing 10/10 leg pain unresponsive to opioids with exquisite pain on passive ankle dorsiflexion where compartment pressure measures 45 mmHg requiring immediate emergent bivalving of cast and four-compartment fasciotomy.
Objective/Exam findings: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Acute Compartment Syndrome Lower Extremity Fracture.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute Compartment Syndrome.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Simple post-fracture pain without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Pain out of proportion to the injury, especially with passive stretch — the earliest and most reliable sign.
management_principles: Immediately loosen or bivalve constricting casts or dressings, keep the limb at heart level, and obtain emergent surgical fasciotomy for clinically diagnosed compartment syndrome
Refer to specialty team and provide comprehensive patient counseling
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.objective: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Acute Compartment Syndrome Lower Extremity Fracture.
reference_soap.assessment: Clinical presentation highly suggestive of Acute Compartment Syndrome Lower Extremity Fracture.
reference_soap.plan: Immediately bivalve and remove constricting cast material, keep the limb at heart level, and obtain emergent Orthopedic Surgery consultation for four-compartment fasciotomy. Do not delay surgery for repeated pressure measurements when the clinical diagnosis is clear; interpret pressures with the clinical examination and perfusion pressure. Monitor for rhabdomyolysis and renal injury.

teaching.one_liner: Swelling inside a tight fascial compartment (after a fracture) raises pressure high enough to cut off circulation, causing pain out of proportion to the injury and severe pain on passive stretch — a limb-threatening emergency needing immediate fasciotomy.
red_flags: Pain out of proportion to the injury, especially with passive stretch — the earliest and most reliable sign

must_ask.say: Is the pain much worse than you'd expect for this kind of injury, and is it getting worse?
Does it hurt severely when someone moves your toes or ankle for you?
Do you have any numbness or tingling in your foot?
Has your usual pain medication been helping at all?
How long ago was your leg casted, and when did the pain start getting this bad?

history.answer: I broke my lower leg yesterday and got a cast put on, but over the last few hours the pain has become unbearable, like my leg is about to burst open.
I broke my leg about 18 hours ago and the splint was placed, but this excruciating, tightening pain started getting much worse around 6 hours ago.
The worst pain is deep in the front and back of my right lower leg under the cast, but it feels like the whole calf and foot are exploding.
It is a severe, deep, throbbing pressure and tight squeezing feeling, easily a 10 out of 10.
It is constant and unrelenting, and it has steadily escalated every hour since midnight without letting up at all.
Any slight touch, shifting my leg, or moving my toes makes the pain unbearable, and nothing brings any relief.
I have numbness and a tingling, pins-and-needles sensation spreading across the top of my foot and between my big toe and second toe.
Whenever my toes get bumped or bent backwards even a tiny bit, it shoots blinding, agonizing pain right up my calf.
The doctors gave me strong prescription opioid pain pills after casting it, but even after taking two pills it did not touch the pain at all.
I just need you to cut this cast off immediately and give me whatever strong pain medication will actually stop this agony.
The splint went on about 12 hours ago, and within hours my calf felt tighter and tighter until it felt rock-hard inside.
I can barely wiggle my toes, and trying to pull my foot upwards feels extremely weak and excruciatingly painful.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, sweating, or signs of an infection.
No, I have not had any shortness of breath, chest pain, or coughing.
I slipped and fell heavily during a soccer match yesterday afternoon and snapped my right shin bone.
I tried propping my leg up on pillows and taking the prescribed pain medication, but elevating it actually made the burning and tightness feel worse.
No, I have never had any fractures, blood clots, or severe leg pain like this before.
I am in too much agony to sit still or sleep, and I feel like my leg is losing blood flow.
I think this cast was put on way too tight and it's completely choking off the blood supply to my leg.
I'm terrified that if my leg stays numb and suffocated like this, I'll get permanent nerve damage or even lose the leg.
I just need you to cut this cast off immediately and give me whatever strong pain medication will actually stop this agony.
I have no chronic medical conditions like diabetes, high blood pressure, or kidney disease.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been hospitalized prior to yesterday.
I am only on the pain pills they gave me yesterday at the clinic, which was oxycodone, and I do not take any other daily prescriptions or supplements.
I have no known drug or food allergies.
I do not smoke cigarettes or use any nicotine products.
I drink socially, maybe one or two beers on the weekend, but I have not had any alcohol since the injury.
I work as a software engineer and live in an apartment with my partner.
There is no family history of bleeding disorders, blood clotting problems, or vascular diseases.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 142/88 mmHg, heart rate 108 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, temperature 36.8°C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Young male in severe, visible agony, groaning and clutching his immobilized lower extremity, pale and diaphoretic from pain.
The splinted lower leg and calf demonstrate severe, tense, woody swelling with extreme tenderness upon palpation of the compartments.
Passive dorsiflexion of the ankle and passive extension of the toes elicit excruciating, severe pain in the anterior and deep calf compartments.
Hypoesthesia and tingling sensation noted over the first web space of the foot; sensation elsewhere is diminished compared to the contralateral side.
Active extension of the great toe and ankle dorsiflexion are severely weakened and limited by agonizing pain.
Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are palpable but weak bilaterally, with capillary refill in the toes slightly delayed at 3 seconds.
Tense, tight skin visible at the exposed margins of the splint and toes without open wounds or gross skin necrosis.
